source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1999) Illusory inferences: a novel class of erroneous deductions, Exp 1
finding: People drew the predicted invalid conclusion on every illusion problem and were nearly always right on matched controls. They were very confident in both.
numbers: N=16 Princeton students, no logic training. Illusions: 100% predicted invalid conclusion on both problems. Controls: 88% and 100% correct. All 16 better on controls than illusions (sign test P=0.5^16). Confidence 4.4 on illusions vs 4.3 on controls (5-point scale).
limits: Small N, one lab, only two illusion items in Exp 1, one content type (cards, king/ace). Authors wrote the theory and the items.
agent_relevance: A reasoner can be confidently and uniformly wrong on items where the truth of one premise hides the falsity of its alternative. Confidence is no signal of error here (supports G10).

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1999), think-aloud and warning replication by Meyer
finding: A small replication told one group the problems were tricky and asked everyone to think aloud. Both groups kept making the fallacy. The warning only slowed people down. Protocols showed people read 'or else' as a disjunction and still erred.
numbers: No counts reported. Small-scale, informal. Reported as qualitative: both groups continued to make fallacies and get controls right.
limits: No N or percentages given. Report is second-hand inside the main paper.
agent_relevance: A generic 'be careful, it may be a trick' warning does not fix this error class. A targeted procedure is needed (see b09, b10).

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1999), Exp 2 (web)
finding: An explicit rubric (one clue true, one false) did not remove the illusion. A web sample of puzzle fans also fell for it.
numbers: N=20 web users (first 20 from distinct machines). 15/20 inferred 'there is an ace' (the illusion); other 5 chose 'indeterminate'. 15 right on the control, 5 ties. Sign test stated as under 1 in 30 thousand.
limits: Self-selected web sample, no control over behaviour, no demographics. The authors concede this. The correct answer differs between control and illusion.
agent_relevance: The effect survives an explicit statement of the exclusive rule. Instruction text alone is weak protection.

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1999), Exp 3 (exclusive disjunctions, no conditionals)
finding: Illusions appeared with plain 'only one is true' disjunctions and no conditionals. This rules out explanations that depend on how 'if' is read.
numbers: N=40 Princeton students. Illusion 1: 85% fallacy B, 15% 'nothing follows'. Illusions 3 and 4: 63% and 68% fallacy. Control: 98% correct. 33 of 40 drew at least one illusory conclusion and were right on the control; 7 ties.
limits: Exclusive-disjunction problems came last, so practice may have lowered error. Only a few of those who said 'nothing follows' realised the premises were contradictory.
agent_relevance: Item sets are cheap to build in code and give a clean diagnostic: same premises, one question that exposes the error, one that does not.

source: Johnson-Laird & Savary (1999), discussion of rival explanations
finding: The authors list rival accounts (pragmatics, 'or else' read as 'and', programming-language reading of conditionals) and say each fails. Strongest test: identical premises with two different questions, one illusory and one control, give a big gap.
numbers: Cited test (Johnson-Laird & Goldvarg 1997, not opened): 'nearly everyone' said yes to the queen-and-ace question and was right on the king-and-ace control. Think-aloud protocols showed disjunctions read as disjunctions.
limits: Rival refutations are made by the theory's authors. The 1997 study was not opened.
agent_relevance: The same-premise, different-question design is the right pattern for any ablation of our own enumeration step.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2009) Disjunctive illusory inferences and how to eliminate them, Exp 1 and 2 (Memory & Cognition 37)
finding: Embedded disjunctions (A or else (B or else C)) produce illusions of possibility. Control questions on the same premises are mostly correct.
numbers: Exp 1: N=18 online. Correct on illusory problems: 17% (exclusive-exclusive) and 22% (inclusive-exclusive). Controls: 100% and 78%. 16/18 showed the control>illusion gap (binomial p<.005). Exp 2: 40 Princeton community members; controls 93% vs illusions 37% correct (Wilcoxon z=8.94, p<.0001).
limits: Online, small N in Exp 1. Authors' own item sets. The inclusive-inclusive illusion was weak (58% correct).
agent_relevance: Not every nested-disjunction item fools people: the theory's program predicts which. Items need code-generated predictions, not guesswork.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2009), remedial instructions in Exp 2
finding: Instructions telling people to consider what is false gave only partial and uneven help. No reliable overall gain versus the uninstructed group, but the control-illusion gap shrank.
numbers: Instructed vs uninstructed groups: group difference not reliable (Mann-Whitney z=1.7, p=0.09). Interaction (gap smaller when instructed) reliable, z=2.2, p<.05. Illusion accuracy by problem type: instructed 38/38/63/56%, uninstructed 17/21/21/58%. Second block: instructed better, z=2.38, p<.02; first block no difference (p>.2).
limits: Online task; authors suspect people did not apply the instructions. Earlier work (Yang & Johnson-Laird 2000) found instructions that also lowered control accuracy.
agent_relevance: A one-line reminder is not enough. A fixed step that makes the model write the false-case table is a better design than advice.

source: Yang & Johnson-Laird (2000) Illusions in quantified reasoning: how to make the impossible seem possible, and vice versa (Memory & Cognition 28)
finding: Illusions also occur for quantified premises ('at least some X are not red' vs 'none are red'). Illusions of possibility were more convincing than illusions of impossibility.
numbers: Exp 1: N=20 undergraduates: 90% correct on controls, 54% on illusions (slightly above chance). Every participant better on controls. Exp 2 (dyadic relations, N=20): 93% controls vs 51% illusions. Confidence only slightly higher on controls (differences .13 and .32 on a 5-point scale).
limits: N=20 per experiment, one student population, authors' items.
agent_relevance: The illusion pattern is not limited to propositional logic. It generalises to quantifiers, so test sets should include quantified items.

source: Yang & Johnson-Laird (2000) How to eliminate illusions in quantified reasoning (Memory & Cognition 28), Exp 1
finding: First effective antidote: teach people to work out the case where premise 1 is true and premise 2 false. It lifted illusion accuracy but cost control accuracy.
numbers: N=20 Princeton undergraduates. Without instruction: controls 93% vs illusions 33%. With instruction: illusions 33% to 65% (z=3.27, p<.01); controls 93% to 79% (z=2.31, p<.01). Overall 63% to 72% (z=2.10, p<.05).
limits: Gap not closed. The control decline shows a real cost of the procedure, not just practice. Within-subject block order; N small.
agent_relevance: Case-splitting that enumerates 'A true, B false' helps, but it costs accuracy where it is not needed. Gate it by item type (supports G1: run only on a signal).

source: Yang & Johnson-Laird (2000), Exp 2 of the antidote paper
finding: Analysing both cases (premise 1 true and 2 false, then 2 true and 1 false) removed the illusion-control gap. Both converged near 71%.
numbers: N=20 undergraduates. Illusions 39% to 71% (z=3.72, p<.001). Controls 87% to 72% (z=1.99, p<.05). After instruction the illusion-control difference was n.s. (z=0.44). Illusions of impossibility rose 26% to 72%; illusions of possibility 51% to 70%.
quote: An ideal antidote, of course, should result in 100% correct performance with both fallacies and controls.
limits: 71% is far from ideal. The procedure is taxing. Gain partly by lowering controls. Single lab.
agent_relevance: Full enumeration of both truth-assignments is the best-supported fix in this literature, but still leaves about 30% errors. Pair it with a code check, not model self-grading.

source: Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird (2000), as quoted in Yang & Johnson-Laird (2000b)
finding: Asking people to check conclusions against the truth of only one premise gave a large reliable gain, but illusions still occurred on nearly half the trials. Original study not opened; the figure is taken from the secondary text that I did open.
numbers: 57% of conclusions correct after the remedial check, as quoted in Yang & Johnson-Laird 2000b.
limits: Second-hand; original not read.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as b09 and b10: partial gains only from instruction-style fixes.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2017) Illusions in Reasoning (Minds & Machines 27), review
finding: Review of illusion studies across connectives, quantifiers, deontic and causal relations. Says no study failed to give a reliable effect. Lists mitigations: rubric 'only one is false' (Tabossi 1998), prior production of false instances (Newsome & Johnson-Laird 2006), checking against the one-true constraint (Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird 2000).
numbers: One cited study: 128 participants, all but one made more errors with illusions than controls (the one exception made no errors at all).
quote: The occurrence of systematic and predictable fallacies in human reasoning came as a shock to us.
limits: Review by the theory's authors. No independent replication or meta-analysis of illusions is cited, and file-drawer effects cannot be ruled out. 'None failed' is the authors' claim.
agent_relevance: Illusions are the best-attested model-theory prediction but the evidence base is largely one network of labs. Treat effect size as a likely upper bound.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2017), discussion of rival accounts of illusions
finding: Rivals: formal rules (only valid rules, so no systematic fallacy), probability logic, Stenning & van Lambalgen (credulous vs skeptical reasoning), programming-style reading of conditionals, and the erotetic theory of Koralus & Mascarenhas (a variant of the model theory). Only the erotetic theory is credited as also predicting illusions.
numbers: No new numbers. Authors say no alternative theory covers a comprehensive sample of illusions.
limits: Authors judge their rivals. The erotetic theory is framed as a sibling, not a competitor.
agent_relevance: The finding to keep is that the error follows from representing truth only. Which of two sibling theories is right matters little for scaffold design.

source: Koralus & Mascarenhas (2013) The erotetic theory of reasoning, and Mascarenhas & Koralus follow-ups
finding: Sibling account: successive premises are read as questions and maximally strong answers. It predicts novel illusory inferences, including ones with indefinites. Search snippets say neither model theory nor other familiar theories fit the new results. Page text was not retrievable.
numbers: A later paper (search snippet) says acceptance of the standard disjunctive illusion was 80-85% across Walsh & Johnson-Laird 2004 and Mascarenhas & Koralus papers.
limits: Not opened (fetch returned empty). Numbers are from a search snippet. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: A competing explanation exists, but it predicts the same kind of failure. No different scaffold implication.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2012) Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin 138)
finding: Meta-analysis of 7 of 12 theories against 6 data sets of free-response syllogisms. None gave an adequate account. The original mental-models program had high hits and weak correct rejections. Verbal models had the best balance.
numbers: 6 data sets, N=20,20,20,20,20,56 (156 participants). Mental models: 95% hits, 74% correct rejections. Illicit conversion: 44% hits, 93% correct rejections. Verbal models: 63% hits, 90% rejections, 84% overall (marginally heterogeneous, I2=52%). Model-based theories 76% vs heuristic theories 66% overall. Human accuracy per syllogism ranged from 1% to 90% (AI2 90%, AE2 1%). Kendall's W for entropy concordance .45.
limits: Small studies, mostly one lab network (Johnson-Laird & Steedman 1978, Bara, Roberts), student samples. Source-founding theory excluded for lack of predictions. Publication-bias regression significant for model-theory hits (z=2.03, p<.05). Authors are proponents of the model theory.
agent_relevance: Ground truth for how people fail: the same few syllogisms (e.g. AE2, EA1) are wrong for nearly everyone. A scaffold should expect the same fixed-point errors in the model and test for them.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2016) How people differ in syllogistic reasoning (CogSci)
finding: Introduces the mReasoner parameters: model size, atypicality, propensity to search for counterexamples, propensity to weaken a refuted conclusion. It fits the meta-analysis and individual strategy groups.
numbers: Fit to meta-analysis data r=.82. Early study (Johnson-Laird & Steedman 1978, 20 Columbia students) gave 'nothing follows' answers 45% vs 30% in the meta-analysis (z=6.19, p<.001). Bara et al. (1995): among measured factors only working-memory capacity correlated with syllogism performance, a small share of variance.
limits: Four free parameters fitted to the same data, so fits are in-sample. Author-built program.
agent_relevance: The counterexample-search propensity is the key switch. Our agent can control it in code (always search on a signal) instead of relying on the model's habit.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2021) Reasoning about properties: a computational theory (Psychological Review)
finding: Eleven simulations of mReasoner. The best-fitting simulation correlates with the 64-syllogism meta-analysis data. Individuals split into poor (small intuitive models), intermediate and best (large models that search for alternatives) groups.
numbers: Meta-analysis fit r=.80, RMSE=.13. 20 individual participants: mean best-fit r=.70 (range .57-.86), mean worst-fit r=.24; all but four best-fits r>=.60 (about 50% of variance). Three groups: r=.78, .83, .91. Poorest group: size 2.0, search .4. Best group: size 4.5, search .8, reconclude .6. Properties-of-individuals task r=.92, RMSE=.15. A table cites meta-analytic prediction accuracy of 89%.
limits: Parameters fitted post hoc. Four free parameters against 576 data cells. No out-of-sample prediction in the pages read. Authors' own theory and software.
agent_relevance: Good evidence that deliberate counterexample search separates good from poor reasoners, but only as a description fitted after the fact.

source: Ragni, Riesterer, Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2018) Individuals become more logical without feedback (CogSci)
finding: People re-tested a week later on all 64 syllogisms got better without feedback. mReasoner explains this as more counterexample search.
numbers: N=20. Correct 58% to 68% from test 1 to test 2; 19/20 improved (binomial p<.0001). Mean 27.5 changed conclusions per person. 95.9% of changes kept polarity. mReasoner fit 60% of inferences in week 1 and 65% in week 2.
limits: N=20, one data set, same population as the 1978 study. Gain was similar for valid and no-valid-conclusion items here, which the larger retest did not find (b19).
agent_relevance: Experience on a task class can raise performance with no external signal, so a within-task adaptation loop is plausible. It needs a held-out check (G3).

source: Dames, Klauer & Ragni (2021) The stability of syllogistic reasoning performance over time (Thinking & Reasoning)
finding: Independent-lab larger retest. People improved within session 1 and not further in session 2. The gain was only for valid syllogisms, not for no-valid-conclusion items. This partly fails to replicate b18.
numbers: N=100, two sessions one week apart. Mean accuracy 50.1% (SD 18.7). Observed gain between sessions 2.6% (model estimate 52.7% to 58.2%, i.e. 5.5%; valid items 8.2%). Mean RT 14.85 s then 12.14 s. 53% reported using a strategy. Raven score predicted accuracy (OR 1.96, p<.001) and the improvement on invalid items (3-way interactions OR 1.10, p=.009 and OR 1.25, p=.003). Working memory, cognitive reflection, Need for Cognition and Big Five did not predict change after correction.
limits: German university sample, online. Different task format from b18. The authors suggest the gain on valid items reflects less bias to say 'nothing follows', not better counterexample search.
agent_relevance: The likeliest practice gain is a shift in response bias, not deeper checking. Adding practice or in-context examples may only move that bias (see b24).

source: Ragni & Kola (2018) On selecting evidence to test hypotheses: a theory of selection tasks (Psychological Bulletin)
finding: Meta-analysis of 228 Wason selection-task experiments. Card choices are not independent. The model theory fits better than the one remaining rival. Feedback pushes people from picking confirming instances to picking counterexamples.
numbers: 228 experiments, of which 99 reported all 16 possible selections. Mean informativeness 2.14 bits (max 4). Real experiments were more redundant than 10,000 independent-choice simulations of each (Wilcoxon tests, three content types). Feedback in the repeated selection task moved choices toward counterexamples.
limits: The rival inference-guessing model had its 10 parameters cut to fit canonical selections, so the comparison is partly constrained by the authors. The authors admit free parameters trade explanation for description. Authors are theory proponents.
agent_relevance: Two supported facts: (1) the default is to look for confirming instances; (2) feedback from real outcomes turns that into counterexample search (supports G2, G3).

source: Ragni, Dames & Johnson-Laird (2019) A meta-analysis of conditional reasoning (CogSci)
finding: 39 experiments compared five theories on patterns of the four conditional inferences. The best theory depends on the task: mental models for producing conclusions; a directional variant for evaluating a given conclusion; the exclusive suppositional theory for picking from options.
numbers: 39 experiments from 15 studies, 2378 participants. Most frequent pattern: accept all four (MP, MT, AC, DA). Next: MP and MT only. Response patterns were more redundant than 10,000 simulations per experiment, which the authors say rules out theories with independent inferences, such as the probabilistic theory of Oaksford et al. (2000).
limits: Written by model-theory authors. Fits compared by BIC using the theory trees from Oberauer (2006). The BIC table came out garbled in the text, so only the ordering is recorded. Task type changes the verdict, so there is no single winner.
agent_relevance: No single theory wins across tasks. The question format (produce vs evaluate vs choose) changes the error pattern, so an agent's prompts should keep format fixed when comparing arms.

source: Oberauer (2006) Reasoning with conditionals: a test of formal models of four theories (Cognitive Psychology 53)
finding: Independent test of four theories on large data sets. Best accounts came from a modified mental-model theory with directionality and a dual-process model. The probabilistic theory did worse. Seen only in a search-result abstract.
numbers: Two large data sets (abstract conditionals; causal and non-causal pseudo-realistic). No figures recorded.
limits: Not opened. Abstract paraphrase from a search result.
agent_relevance: Supports the mixed picture in b21: a model-theory variant holds up, but only with add-ons (directionality, dual process).

source: Singmann, Klauer & Kellen (2014) Intuitive logic revisited: new data and a Bayesian mixed model meta-analysis (PLoS ONE)
finding: A claim built on the idea that an implicit initial mental model makes valid conclusions feel more fluent (people like valid conclusions more). It replicated, then vanished once conclusion content was randomly assigned to valid and invalid. A Bayesian mixed-model meta-analysis favoured no validity effect.
numbers: New Exp 1: 26 completed, 22 analysed (UK, online). Re-analysis of 3 studies with randomised conclusions: the best model had no validity effect; evidence against the best model with a validity effect was described as very strong. Original claim: liking ratings higher for valid than invalid in 4 experiments.
limits: Tests the fluency idea, a spin-off of model theory, not the core theory. Small new sample. A failed replication of a derived claim. Author names taken from the page header only in part (Singmann confirmed).
agent_relevance: Do not trust 'intuitive' detection of validity. Content confounds can fake it. Randomise content in our evaluations.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt & Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of LLMs as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: Zero-shot CoT, in-context learning (ICL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on 64 syllogism schemas with pseudo-words or believable/unbelievable content. Models rarely say 'nothing follows'. ICL helps valid items and hurts consistency. SFT removes most biases. The Atmosphere heuristic predicts model answers.
numbers: Human: 44.63% valid, 40.97% invalid (from Khemlani & Johnson-Laird 2012). LLaMA-3 70B-instruct: 41.25% overall, 32.50% invalid. LLaMA-3 70B base: 30.63% overall, 10.28% invalid, 58.89% valid believable, 54.07% valid unbelievable. Correlation with human item pattern up to .80-.87. Atmosphere theory predicts 92.31% of correct valid answers and 82.97% of errors on invalid (62.79% on valid) for LLaMA-3 8B zero-shot CoT. ICL raised contradictory answers. SFT near ceiling on pseudo-word items.
limits: Open models up to 70B, not frontier. Fine-tuning is out of scope for our no-training scaffold. Pythia SFT overproduced 'nothing follows' (73.91% contradictions, 70.47% from it).
agent_relevance: Models fail like humans on invalid items: they pick an answer from the premise form. A code-side check that enumerates models and says 'nothing follows' when a counterexample exists is the missing piece (G2, G3).

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste & Linzen (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: PaLM 2 models beat humans on average, show the figural (ordering) effect and the same top three syllogism fallacies as humans, rarely say 'nothing follows', and larger models look more like high-deliberation mReasoner settings.
numbers: Human mean accuracy about 50%; best LM about 75%. Largest model slightly below second-largest. Humans: only 3% correct on one syllogism (no A are B, all B are C). mReasoner grid: 1296 settings, 923 finished; first principal component 77% of behavioural variance, loads on the System 2 parameter. With correct answers zeroed, PC1 correlates .6 with the System 2 parameter and below .15 with the rest. Replicated with Llama 2.
limits: Early arXiv version had a sampling bug (fixed in v2). Zero-shot CoT only, 30 samples at temperature 0.5. The 'deliberative' reading is the authors' mapping onto mReasoner.
agent_relevance: Direct model-side evidence that LLM errors on syllogisms are partly model-theory-like (single-model intuitive answers, weak counterexample search). Checks that add counterexamples may transfer.

source: Khemlani, Lotstein & Johnson-Laird (2012) The probabilities of unique events (PLoS ONE 7)
finding: Estimates of P(A and B) often split the difference between P(A) and P(B), violating the probability calculus. Verbal estimates violated it less often.
numbers: Exp 1: N=39 online (Mechanical Turk, native English). Estimates violated a consistent joint distribution on 56% of trials; all 39 participants did so at least once. Exp 2: N=18; violations on 34% of verbal and 68% of numeric judgments (Wilcoxon z=3.55, p<.0005). Theory fit r=.76, RMSE .14.
limits: Online convenience samples. The violations also fit older conjunction-fallacy and anchoring accounts. Authors' program not independently tested.
agent_relevance: Probability combination by the model is unreliable. Matches G5: compute and normalise probabilities in code.

source: Ragni & Johnson-Laird (2018) Reasoning about possibilities: human reasoning violates all normal modal logics (CogSci)
finding: Judgments about possibility match a model-based theory far better than modal logic System K. People accept inferences that K calls invalid and reject ones it calls valid.
numbers: Exp 1: participants made 80% of the model theory's predicted evaluations vs 56% for modal logic (Wilcoxon z=6.1, p<.000001). Where they disagree: model-theory 'Yes' occurred on 84% vs 16% for logic; model-theory 'No' on 81% vs 19%. r2 with results .99 for the model theory vs .01 for logic (item level). Exp 2: 83% of model-theory conclusions drawn vs 50% for logic.
limits: N not captured from the pages read. Online procedure. The r2 of .99 is at item level, so inflated. Authors built the theory and ran the tests.
agent_relevance: Humans reason parsimoniously about possibilities. An agent that follows full modal logic will disagree with human labels on such items. Pick the norm per benchmark.

source: Johnson-Laird (2024) Mistakes in thinking about cognitive science and how to reduce them (commentary)
finding: Describes a 'model method': a two-minute training in drawing the possibilities for premises. Reports large accuracy and speed gains, even without paper.
numbers: Reported, not new data: trained participants 95% correct vs 63% for controls; 15 s vs 24 s mean per inference; 2 minutes of teaching. Original is Victoria Bell's study (not opened).
limits: Author-recalled result from a commentary, no N, no data, original unread. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If true, the cheapest known fix is to make the reasoner list possibilities explicitly. It still needs our own test (G7).

source: Newstead, Handley & Buck (1999) Falsifying mental models, and Newstead et al. (1992) belief bias, via search summary
finding: An independent group tested whether people build alternative models. A search summary says some people do not go beyond the first model and others do; belief bias is explained by stopping when a believable conclusion fits the first model. A rival (Quayle & Ball) has no falsification step.
numbers: No numbers retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Only a search summary. Do not cite numbers.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in whether the reasoner looks for a second model is the stable mechanism claim. It argues for forcing the search in code.
